content: To ensure continuous availability of expertise, a poisons information center must employ a sufficient number of trained specialists in toxicology. This staffing level should guarantee that at least one specialist is on duty at all times. In practice, the center should also account for staff absences due to illness, holidays, or professional training by maintaining an adequate workforce. The required number of staff depends on factors such as the center's operating hours, the volume and complexity of inquiries, and the number of calls per 1,000 people served. Additionally, staffing levels should be adjusted to accommodate busier periods, as the frequency of inquiries can vary daily and weekly. Each center must tailor its services to meet local needs, and as the center grows, the number of staff may need to increase. Specialists may also be required to undertake additional tasks, such as research, writing substance datasheets, developing treatment protocols, or conducting follow-up studies, necessitating further staffing adjustments. The poisons information center should ideally be led by a director with expertise in clinical toxicology. If the director's role is primarily administrative, a dedicated medical toxicologist should support them. The director is fully responsible for the center's operations and should be employed full-time. They must possess strong leadership qualities, the ability to supervise staff, and maintain good relationships with colleagues and stakeholders. The director should also promote research, secure funding, and oversee the center's development. They, or the supporting medical toxicologist, should take responsibility for clinical governance and define research priorities. Depending on the center's size and requirements, an administrative or operations manager may be necessary to oversee financial resources, equipment, staff schedules, and routine personnel matters. The roles of the director and administrative manager should be clearly defined. Specialists in poisons information are often the first point of contact for inquiries. They provide timely and accurate information and advice to enquirers. These specialists are typically clinical toxicologists with diverse backgrounds, including medicine, pharmacy, nursing, chemistry, life sciences, and veterinary science. In some countries, only physicians are authorized to provide medical advice, requiring specialists to be trained medical doctors. Nurses in this role should ideally have experience managing poisoned patients, especially if the center is associated with a clinical toxicology unit. The knowledge and skills required for this role are highly specialized and not typically covered in other clinical or scientific fields, making in-house training and assessment essential. Continuous training is necessary to keep staff updated on developments in toxicology, and training should lead to recognized qualifications. Collaboration with other poison centers to develop transferable qualifications is encouraged. Once trained, specialists should be able to provide tailored information and advice using the center's databases and agreed patient management protocols. They must also be proficient in operating computer systems, recording inquiries and cases in a standardized manner, and consulting senior colleagues or medical toxicologists when necessary. Specialists contribute to service improvement by analyzing collected data and participating in toxicology research. They should engage in all center activities, including answering inquiries, preparing documentation, evaluating data, and conducting literature searches. Regular team discussions of interesting cases and toxicological problems should be encouraged to promote a harmonized approach to poisoning management. Networking with other poison centers for periodic meetings and information exchange is also beneficial. Medical toxicologists are physicians with specialized training and experience in managing poisoning cases. They may also have expertise in emergency medicine, pediatrics, public health, internal medicine, intensive care, or forensic medicine. Clinical experience in occupational and environmental diseases caused by chemicals is relevant. Experience in toxicological research is valuable, and clinical management of poisoned patients is essential. In some countries, clinical toxicology is not recognized as a medical specialty but may be a subspecialty of clinical pharmacology or occupational medicine. In lowand middle-income countries, recruiting trained medical toxicologists can be challenging, and centers may rely on other healthcare professionals, such as nurses or pharmacists with toxicology training. Centers in such countries should foster the development of this specialty through training, research, and collaboration. Medical toxicologists may provide front-line poisons information services or handle complex cases referred by specialists. They are involved in training specialists and trainees in toxicology and often teach toxicology in hospitals, medical faculties, or universities. They must stay updated on developments in clinical, analytical, and experimental toxicology and systematically collect and evaluate clinical observations to build the evidence base for practice. Support staff, such as administrators, may assist with appointments, meetings, and administrative duties. As poison centers rely on electronic databases, IT specialists may be required to manage these systems. Maintenance and cleaning of equipment and facilities are essential and may be the responsibility of the center or the host institution. Security measures, such as guards, may be necessary, especially for staff working alone at night. Specialist advisers provide medical or non-medical expertise to the center. These advisers may include pediatricians, psychiatrists, teratologists, veterinarians, and toxinologists. Centers in regions with common envenoming or poisoning by animals should have access to experts in these fields. Botanists and mycologists can assist in identifying toxic plants and fungi. Formal agreements should define the roles and availability of these advisers, and periodic joint scientific meetings can strengthen relationships. Access to epidemiological expertise is valuable for surveillance and toxicovigilance. Poisons information centers must have access to databases containing information on substances, products, and poisoning cases. These databases should include evaluations of toxicity, poisoning features, and treatment. Centers may need to compile data on locally important agents, which involves literature research and case data reviews. Product information is a critical component, and centers should establish mechanisms to obtain data from manufacturers and suppliers. Supplementary resources, such as reference books and journals, are also necessary. Pictorial information can aid in identifying tablets, plants, fungi, and animals. Systematic data collection from poisoning inquiries is essential for the center's operations and contributes to its workload.
